Toxoplasmosis Treatment: Lymphadenopathic Toxoplasmosis: Treatment is rarely indicated in immunocompetent adults as this form of the disease is typically self-limiting. Ocular Disease in Adults: The preferred regimen includes pyrimethamine 100 mg as a loading dose on the first day, followed by 25–50 mg daily, combined with sulfadiazine 1 g four times daily and folinic acid (leucovorin) 5–25 mg with each dose of pyrimethamine. Ocular Disease in Pediatrics: The preferred regimen includes pyrimethamine 2 mg/kg on the first day, then 1 mg/kg daily, combined with sulfadiazine 50 mg/kg twice daily and folinic acid (leucovorin) 7.5 mg daily for 4–6 weeks, followed by reevaluation of the patient’s condition. An alternative regimen includes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX). If the patient has a hypersensitivity reaction to sulfa drugs, pyrimethamine and clindamycin can be used instead. 3. Maternal and Fetal Toxoplasmosis: First and Early Second Trimesters: Spiramycin is recommended. Late Second and Third Trimesters: Pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin are recommended for women with acute Toxoplasma gondii infection diagnosed during gestation. Infants: If the infant is likely infected, treatment typically includes pyrimethamine, atovaquone, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin. Congenitally infected newborns are generally treated with pyrimethamine, a sulfonamide, and leucovorin for one year. 4. Toxoplasma Gondii Encephalitis in AIDS: Acute Infection Treatment: Preferred regimen: Pyrimethamine 200 mg orally once, followed by weight-based therapy. For patients <60 kg, pyrimethamine 50 mg daily, sulfadiazine 1000 mg every 6 hours, and leucovorin 10–25 mg daily. For patients ≥60 kg, pyrimethamine 75 mg daily, sulfadiazine 1500 mg every 6 hours, and leucovorin 10–25 mg daily. Leucovorin doses can be increased to 50 mg daily or twice daily if needed. Treatment duration is at least 6 weeks, with longer durations for extensive disease or incomplete response. Alternative regimens include combinations of pyrimethamine, leucovorin, and clindamycin; TMP-SMX; atovaquone with pyrimethamine and leucovorin; or atovaquone with sulfadiazine. Chronic Maintenance Therapy: Preferred regimen: Pyrimethamine 25–50 mg daily, sulfadiazine 2000–4000 mg daily (in 2–4 divided doses), and leucovorin 10–25 mg daily. Alternative regimens include combinations of clindamycin, TMP-SMX, or atovaquone with pyrimethamine and leucovorin. Adjunctive corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) should only be used when clinically indicated to treat mass effect or edema associated with focal lesions and should be discontinued as soon as feasible. Anticonvulsants should be administered to patients with a history of seizures but not used prophylactically. If clindamycin is used instead of sulfadiazine, additional therapy must be added to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). 5. Toxoplasma Gondii Prophylaxis: Indications: Prophylaxis is recommended for Toxoplasma IgG-positive patients with a CD4 count <100 cells/µL. Seronegative patients receiving PCP prophylaxis not active against toxoplasmosis should have Toxoplasma serology retested if the CD4 count declines to <100 cells/µL. Prophylaxis should be initiated if seroconversion occurs. Prophylactic Therapy: Preferred regimen: TMP-SMX 1 double-strength tablet daily. Alternative regimens include TMP-SMX three times weekly, TMP-SMX single-strength daily, or combinations of dapsone with pyrimethamine and leucovorin. Atovaquone alone or with pyrimethamine and leucovorin is also an option. 6. African Trypanosomiasis (Sleeping Sickness): East African Trypanosomiasis: T. b. rhodesiense, Hemolymphatic Stage: Adults are treated with suramin 1 g IV on days 1, 3, 5, 14, and 21. Pediatric patients receive suramin 20 mg/kg IV on the same schedule. T. b. rhodesiense, CNS Involvement: Adults and pediatric patients are treated with melarsoprol 2–3.6 mg/kg/day IV for 3 days, followed by a 7-day break, then another 3-day course, repeated for a total of three series. West African Trypanosomiasis: T. b. gambiense, Hemolymphatic Stage: Adults and pediatric patients are treated with pentamidine 4 mg/kg/day IM or IV for 7–10 days. Pentamidine should only be used during pregnancy and lactation if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk. T. b. gambiense, CNS Involvement: Adults and pediatric patients are treated with eflornithine 400 mg/kg/day in 4 doses for 14 days. Eflornithine should only be used during pregnancy and lactation if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk. Its safety in children has not been established, and it is not FDA-approved for pediatric use. 7. Chagas Disease: Preferred regimen (1): Benznidazole for patients <12 years: 5–7.5 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses for 60 days. For patients ≥12 years: 5–7 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses for 60 days. Preferred regimen (2): Nifurtimox for patients ≤10 years: 15–20 mg/kg/day orally in 3 or 4 divided doses for 90 days. For patients aged 11–16 years: 12.5–15 mg/kg/day orally in 3 or 4 divided doses for 90 days.
